title: Shoot the Moon — launch film (VO/picture lock review)
thesis: I wanted to build an original browser game about lunar territory, escalation and orbital warfare. The story is not that AI made a game: it is that frontier models, directed as creative and engineering collaborators, let one person execute an original idea, visual direction and system design far faster than they could alone.

voiceover.text: Getting there first feels like it should count for something.
It doesn't.
So you decide how far you're willing to go.
Then it's their turn.
And while you're busy with each other, someone else shows up.
I've wanted to make something like this since I was a kid playing StarCraft, reading Dune, and searching the library for anything I could find about space.
Shoot the Moon became my version of all of that: territory, machines, escalation, and a Moon that actually feels enormous.
And none of this is a cutscene. It's the game running live in a browser, built for a phone as much as a desktop.
Every site exists at a real latitude and longitude on a lunar sphere.
One of the key moments that changed the project was realizing how good the frontier models had become at math.

We used that to work out flight paths around the Moon, validate a hundred-and-thirty-two-degree route at two thousand and forty-eight points, and design camera moves I probably would have never even tried.
Then I started pushing the visual side harder.
The monuments, machines, and animations are all built in code.
The mass driver is still one of my favorites. It started as an idea in my head and gradually became this huge mechanical thing that actually feels like it belongs on the Moon.
I didn't ask a model to invent this. I already knew the game I wanted to make.
Claude and Codex became collaborators I could direct, test, and challenge.
My background in QA helped more than I expected. I treated every feature like something that had to survive testing, not just look right once.
Bad captures got recaptured. Bugs got reproduced. Ideas got rejected and rebuilt.
What I'm proudest of isn't that models wrote code.
It's that this feels like the kind of game I used to imagine making.
And now everyone can play it.

claims.claim: Runs live in a browser; React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber.
Built for a phone as much as a desktop; same game and rules on a phone viewport with touch input.
evidence: src/app/CounterstrikeHud.tsx ("TAP ONCE WHILE THE AMBER RINGS ALIGN")
claims.caveat: README: physical Android device acceptance (frame pacing, thermals) is still open. The film claims phone-first design, not device performance.

claims.claim: Every site is a real latitude and longitude on a lunar sphere, in metres.
evidence: capture/youtube/captures/landing-site-panel.png (LATITUDE 5.490° N · LONGITUDE 16.040° W · MEAN SPHERE · ALT 0 M)

claims.claim: The missile flies a route computed between the two sites, 132° apart, peaking at 760 km, never below 24 km, tested at 2,048 points.
evidence: e2e/firstStrikeFixtures.ts (canonical site 0.248 rad, -0.684 rad, 18 m = 14.209° N 39.190° W)
claims.note: All numbers on the board are computed at render time by capture/youtube/routeDiagram.ts calling the game code.

claims.claim: No imported 3D model files; every machine is written in TypeScript.
Frontier models (Claude, OpenAI Codex) used as collaborators in a Codespaces-based workflow, directed by the author.
evidence: docs/SHOOT_THE_MOON_MOTION_CHAMPIONSHIP_HANDOFF.md (two model treatments, resolved direction, implementation brief)

claims.claim: The First Strike went from a red rocket and a white disc to the physical, directed look by iterating against a written visual contract.
evidence: artifacts/release-candidate/README.md (baseline at d377cb5 vs release-candidate final)

claims.claim: All gameplay was captured deterministically from the game and checked frame by frame.
evidence: capture/README.md "Frame stepping" and Phase 6 (each output frame matched to its planned source)
capture/runner.ts (frame counter must advance; never silently duplicates)

claims.claim: A capture with the title screen ghosting through the FIRST STRIKE COMPLETE card was caught and recaptured rather than hidden.
evidence: capture/README.md (dismissLaunchGate waits for the gate fade; c12 recaptured)

why.title-screen: Act 3 has to show that this is a live browser game, not an animation. The reel has no shot of the game's own entry screen; this is the current build's real launch gate.
why.landing-site-panel: The coordinate claim must be visible. The game itself prints the selected site's latitude, longitude and altitude; the reel never shows that panel.
why.mining-laser-closeup: Territory and construction: the reel shows no mining or base economy at all. This is the live outpost HUD with the robot's laser on a deposit, and it carries the zero-model-files claim.
why.helios-mechanical-peak: Explicit fourth-capture authorization in the VO/picture lock brief: the original c22 is only 1.8s, inadequate for the 12.22s selected personal mass-driver line.
